topics.title: Agent & Tool Security
topics.description: Agent and tool security limits what an agent can do if it is misled or makes a mistake. Practices include giving each tool the least permissions it needs, running code in a sandbox, requiring human approval for risky actions such as deleting data or sending money, and treating tool results as untrusted input. Tool outputs can carry injected instructions.
resources: GitHub MCP Exploited: Accessing Private Repositories via MCP - Invariant Labs
Human in the Loop - Cloudflare Agents

topics.title: Agent
topics.description: An agent is a system where an LLM decides its own next steps in a loop. It calls tools, reads the results and continues until the goal is reached. This differs from a fixed workflow, where the steps are decided in advance by the developer. Coding assistants and research assistants are common examples.

topics.title: Agents
topics.description: AI agents are autonomous systems that use LLMs to reason, plan, and take actions to achieve specific goals. They combine language understanding with tool usage, memory, and decision-making to perform complex, multi-step tasks. Agents can interact with external APIs and services while maintaining context across interactions.

topics.title: AI Red Teaming
topics.description: AI red teaming involves deliberately testing AI systems to find vulnerabilities, biases, or harmful behaviors through adversarial prompting. Teams attempt to make models produce undesired outputs, bypass safety measures, or exhibit problematic behaviors. This process helps identify weaknesses and improve AI safety and robustness before deployment.
resources: Open the AI Red Teaming roadmap

topics.title: AI vs AGI
topics.description: AI (Artificial Intelligence) refers to systems that perform specific tasks intelligently, while AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) represents hypothetical AI with human-level reasoning across all domains. Current LLMs are narrow AI - powerful at language tasks but lacking true understanding or general intelligence like AGI would possess.

topics.title: Anatomy of Context
topics.description: The context is everything the model sees in one request. It usually includes the system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents, memory, the conversation history and the latest user message. Each part uses tokens from the same window. Knowing what is in the context helps you find why a model behaves a certain way.
resources: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic

topics.title: Anthropic
topics.description: Anthropic develops Claude, a family of large language models focused on safety and helpfulness. The current lineup includes Claude Opus 4.7 (most capable, for complex reasoning and agentic coding), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (best speed-intelligence balance), and Claude Haiku 4.5 (fastest, near-frontier intelligence). All models support extended thinking, vision, and 1M token context windows.

topics.title: Automatic Prompt Engineering
topics.description: Automatic prompt engineering uses a model or an optimization tool to generate, test and select better prompts. You give it a task, example inputs and a way to score outputs, and it tries many variations. Frameworks such as DSPy follow this approach. Results depend on having a good eval set to score against.

topics.title: Building Eval Sets
topics.description: An eval set is a collection of test inputs, often with expected outputs or scoring criteria. Good sets include typical cases, edge cases and past failures. They start small, with a few dozen examples, and grow as new problems appear. They are the base for comparing prompts and models.
resources: Define success criteria and build evaluations - Anthropic
Demystifying evals for AI agents - Anthropic
LLM evaluation metrics and methods, explained simply - Evidently AI

topics.title: Calibrating LLMs
topics.description: Calibration is how well a model's stated confidence matches how often it is right. LLMs often sound certain when they are wrong. You can ask for a confidence score or a set of levels, then compare these against real outcomes and set thresholds, for example sending low-confidence answers to a human.

topics.title: Chain of Thought (CoT)
topics.description: Chain of thought prompting asks the model to write out its reasoning steps before giving the final answer, for example by adding "think step by step" or by showing worked examples. It improves results on math, logic and multi-step problems. On reasoning models it is usually unnecessary, because they already think before answering.
resources: What is chain of thought (CoT) prompting? - IBM
Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models - arXiv
Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering: Smarter AI with RAG & Agents

topics.title: Classification & Routing
topics.description: Classification and routing use a first model call to decide what a request is, then send it to the right prompt, model or tool. The prompt lists the options with clear descriptions, keeps them from overlapping and includes an "other" choice for unclear input. Code then reads the label and acts on it. Examples include support ticket triage and sending easy questions to a smaller model.

topics.title: CLAUDE.md & AGENTS.md
topics.description: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are markdown files kept in a project that coding agents read at the start of each session. They hold standing instructions such as build and test commands, code conventions and rules for the project. AGENTS.md is an open format used by several tools, and CLAUDE.md is the file Claude Code reads. Short, specific instructions work better than long ones.
resources: Does Cursor read AGENTS.md, and should you use it or Cursor rules?

topics.title: Context Budgeting
topics.description: Context budgeting is deciding how many tokens each part of the context gets. System prompt, tools, retrieved documents, history and the model's reply all compete for the same window and add to cost and latency. A budget forces choices about what to keep, trim or retrieve on demand, and it helps keep quality steady in long-running tasks.
resources: LLM Cost Optimization: 5 Levers That Cut API Spend 70-85% - Morph
The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost - DigitalOcean

topics.title: Context Compaction
topics.description: Context compaction shortens the context when it grows too long. The usual method is to summarize older conversation turns or tool results and keep only the important facts, decisions and open tasks. Some systems also clear old tool outputs. It frees space and cuts cost, but a bad summary can lose details the model needs later.

topics.title: Context Evaluation
topics.description: Context evaluation checks whether the information given to the model is good, separately from the prompt. For RAG systems this means asking whether retrieval found the right documents, and whether the answer is supported by them. Measuring these two parts separately shows whether a failure comes from retrieval or from generation.
resources: AI Agent Evaluation - Machine Learning Mastery
RAGAS: How to Evaluate a RAG Application

topics.title: Context Failure Modes
topics.description: Context failure modes are common ways that context causes bad output. Poisoning is when a wrong fact enters the context and keeps being reused. Distraction is when too much detail pulls the model away from the task. Confusion is when irrelevant material misleads it, and clash is when parts of the context contradict each other. Each one has a different fix.
resources: How Long Contexts Fail - Drew Breunig
Understanding LLM Failure Modes (And Why They Matter More Than the Model Itself) - Medium

topics.title: Context Isolation
topics.description: Context isolation gives each sub-task or sub-agent its own separate context. A sub-agent does a focused job, such as searching or reviewing, and returns only a short result to the main agent. This keeps noise and mistakes from spreading and keeps the main context small.
resources: 4 context engineering strategies every AI engineer needs to know - Owain Lewis

topics.title: Context Rot
topics.description: Context rot is the drop in output quality as the context gets longer, even when it is within the window limit. Models can miss or misuse information buried in the middle of long inputs, and irrelevant text adds noise. The practical lesson is to keep context short and relevant rather than filling the window.
resources: How Long Contexts Fail - Drew Breunig
Coding Agents Don't Need Bigger Context Windows - Towards Data Science
Why LLMs get dumb (Context Windows Explained)

topics.title: Context Security
topics.description: Context security protects the information that goes into the context window. It covers untrusted retrieved content, poisoned documents, and secrets or personal data that should not be exposed in a prompt or reply. The main practice is keeping trusted instructions separate from untrusted content and limiting what sensitive data enters the context at all.
resources: Context Engineering Is Security Engineering. RSA 2026 Made the Case. - Zenity
When Data Becomes Instructions: AI Agents Need a Chain of Custody for Context - Check Point

topics.title: Context Sources
topics.description: Context sources are the places where information in the context comes from. Common ones are user input, documents, databases, APIs, tool results, previous conversations and stored memory. Each source differs in reliability, freshness and cost, so deciding which ones to use and when is a core part of context engineering.
resources: The Context Layer for AI: What Enterprises Get Wrong - DataHub
Context Engineering for AI Agents: The Complete Guide - Medium
Most devs don't understand how context windows work

topics.title: Context Window
topics.description: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in one request. It covers the prompt, the conversation history, any retrieved material and the model's own reply. Text beyond the limit has to be cut or left out. Larger windows allow more material, although quality can drop as they fill up.
resources: What is a context window? - IBM
Why LLMs get dumb (Context Windows Explained)

topics.title: Context Window
topics.description: Context window refers to the maximum number of tokens an LLM can process in a single interaction, including both input prompt and generated output. When exceeded, older parts are truncated. Understanding this constraint is crucial for prompt engineering—you must balance providing sufficient context with staying within token limits.
resources: What is a context window? - IBM

topics.title: Contextual Prompting
topics.description: Contextual prompting means adding background information the model needs for the task, such as who the audience is, what has happened so far or what constraints apply. Without it the model has to guess. It is the small-scale version of context engineering: deciding which facts to include in one prompt.
resources: Prompt Structure and Key Parts - LearnPrompting
What is Context in Prompt Engineering? - God of Prompt

topics.title: Controlling Outputs
topics.description: Controlling outputs means shaping the format, length, style and variability of a model's response. Some controls are written in the prompt, such as asking for JSON. Others are API settings, such as maximum tokens or temperature. Applications that read the output with code need these controls to get consistent results.
resources: Mastering Prompt Engineering: Format, Length, and Audience - Techlasi

topics.title: Delimiters & XML Tags
topics.description: Delimiters are markers such as triple backticks, quotes or headings that separate one part of a prompt from another. XML tags like `<document>` and `<instructions>` do the same job and give each part a name you can refer to. They help the model distinguish instructions from data, and they make it harder for text inside the data to be mistaken for a command.
resources: Use XML tags to structure your prompts - Anthropic

topics.title: Effort Levels
topics.description: Effort levels control how much a reasoning model thinks before it answers. Providers expose this as a level such as low, medium or high, or as a token budget for thinking, and the names differ between them. More effort improves results on hard problems but increases cost and latency. For simple tasks a low setting is usually enough.
resources: What is a reasoning model? - IBM

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.description: Embeddings are lists of numbers that represent the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning end up close together. Systems use them for semantic search: embed the documents and the query, then return the nearest matches. RAG pipelines depend on them to find relevant content.
resources: What are Embeddings in Machine Learning? - Cloudflare
RAG Explained: Understanding Embeddings, Similarity, and Retrieval - Towards Data Science

topics.title: Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Eng.
topics.description: Fine-tuning trains a model further on your own examples to change its behavior, while prompt engineering changes only the input. Prompting is faster, cheaper and easy to iterate on, so it is usually the first thing to try. Fine-tuning makes sense when you need a consistent style or format at scale, or a specialized task that prompts cannot reach.
resources: When to use prompt engineering vs. fine-tuning - TechTarget
Prompt Engineering vs Fine Tuning: When to Use Each - Codecademy
RAG vs Fine Tuning: How to Choose the Right Method - Monte Carlo
RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering: Optimizing AI Models

topics.title: Google
topics.description: Google develops Gemini, a family of multimodal AI models. The latest flagship, Gemini 3, supports text, image, video, and audio through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Google also offers specialized models including Imagen for image generation, Veo for video, and Lyria 3 for music. Their research has advanced many prompt engineering techniques, including Chain of Thought reasoning.

topics.title: Grounding
topics.description: Grounding means tying the model's answer to supplied sources. The prompt tells the model to answer only from the provided text, to say when the answer is not there and to quote or cite the passages it used. It is one of the simplest ways to reduce hallucinations, and it is the base of most RAG applications.

topics.title: Hallucination
topics.description: A hallucination is when a model produces false or unsupported information in a confident tone. It happens because models generate likely text and do not check facts. Grounding answers in provided sources, asking for citations and verifying important outputs all reduce it.

topics.title: Improving Prompts
topics.description: Improving prompts is the loop of testing, finding failures and changing the prompt. The usual habit is to change one thing at a time and rerun the eval set, so you know what caused any difference. This can be done by hand or with tools that help automate the search.
resources: ChatGPT Prompt Engineering for Developers - DeepLearning.AI

topics.title: Introduction
topics.description: Prompt engineering is the practice of writing inputs that get useful, reliable outputs from a large language model. Context engineering widens the view to everything the model sees: instructions, retrieved documents, tool definitions, memory and conversation history. This roadmap starts with writing good prompts, moves on to managing context, and ends with evaluation and safety.
resources: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic

topics.title: Jailbreaks
topics.description: A jailbreak is a prompt that gets a model to break its own safety rules and produce content it would normally refuse. Common methods include role-play scenarios, encoded text and long multi-turn pressure. Providers train against known jailbreaks, but new ones keep appearing, so applications should not rely on the model's refusals alone.
resources: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections - Anthropic
Prompt Injection vs. Jailbreaking: What's the Difference? - Learn Prompting
Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail? - arXiv

topics.title: JSON Schema
topics.description: JSON Schema is a standard way to describe the fields, types and required values of a JSON object. Many model APIs accept a schema and constrain the response to match it, so the output always parses and has the expected fields. The same format is used to define tool and function calls. A very strict schema can reduce answer quality, and support varies between models.
resources: How do Structured Outputs Work? - Cohere

topics.title: LLM-as-Judge
topics.description: LLM-as-judge uses a model to score another model's outputs against criteria, such as accuracy, tone or completeness. It scales to many outputs where human review would be slow. Judges can be biased, for example toward longer answers, so clear rubrics are needed and results should be checked against human ratings.
resources: LLM-as-a-judge: a complete guide to using LLMs for evaluations - Evidently AI
LLM-as-a-judge vs. human evaluation: Why together is better - SuperAnnotate
LLM as a Judge: Scaling AI Evaluation Strategies

topics.title: LLM Basics
topics.description: An LLM generates text by predicting the next token from all the tokens before it, then repeating the process. Base models are trained on raw text and simply continue it, while instruct models get extra training to follow instructions and hold conversations. Most models you use through chat apps and APIs are instruct models. Knowing this explains why the wording, examples and context in a prompt change the output.
resources: New to LLMs? Start Here - Towards Data Science
What are large language models (LLMs)? - IBM

topics.title: LLM Self Evaluation
topics.description: LLM self-evaluation involves prompting models to assess their own outputs for quality, accuracy, or adherence to criteria. This technique can identify errors, rate confidence levels, or check if responses meet specific requirements. Self-evaluation helps improve output quality through iterative refinement and provides valuable feedback for prompt optimization.

topics.title: LLM
topics.description: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token. From this one skill it can write, summarize, translate, answer questions and generate code. It produces its output one token at a time, based on the text it has been given.
resources: Differences Between Chatbots and LLMs - LearnPrompting
What is a large language model (LLM)? - Cloudflare

topics.title: LLMs and How They Work
topics.description: LLMs function as sophisticated prediction engines that process text sequentially, predicting the next token based on relationships between previous tokens and patterns from training data. They don't predict single tokens directly but generate probability distributions over possible next tokens, which are then sampled using parameters like temperature and top-K. The model repeatedly adds predicted tokens to the sequence, building responses iteratively. This token-by-token prediction process, combined with massive training datasets, enables LLMs to generate coherent, contextually relevant text across diverse applications and domains.
resources: What are large language models (LLMs)? - IBM
How Large Language Models Work: Explained Simply

topics.title: Long-Context vs RAG
topics.description: Large context windows make it possible to put whole documents into a prompt instead of retrieving pieces. Long context is simpler and works well for a limited set of documents, but it costs more per request and quality can drop as the input grows. RAG scales to large collections and keeps the context small, but depends on retrieval finding the right passages. When using long context, place the documents first and the question last.
resources: What is long context, and why does it matter for your AI? - Google Cloud
Is RAG Dead? The Rise of Context Engineering and Semantic Layers for Agentic AI - Towards Data Science

topics.title: Managing Context
topics.description: Managing context means choosing what goes into the context window, in what order, and what to remove as a task goes on. The goal is to give the model what it needs for the current step and nothing more. Techniques include retrieval, memory, compaction, isolation and caching.
resources: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic
4 context engineering strategies every AI engineer needs to know - Owain Lewis

topics.title: Max Tokens
topics.description: Max tokens sets the largest number of tokens the model can generate in a response. It protects against very long outputs and limits cost. The model does not know about the limit, so a response that hits it is cut off mid-sentence. To get shorter answers that still end properly, ask for a specific length in the prompt too.
resources: Max Tokens - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum

topics.title: MCP
topics.description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. A tool is exposed once as an MCP server and can then be used by any client that supports the protocol, instead of writing a custom integration for each app. Servers can provide tools, resources and prompt templates.
resources: MCP Explained: How Modern AI Agents Connect to the Real World - Towards Data Science
What is MCP? Integrate AI Agents with Databases & APIs

topics.title: Memory & State
topics.description: State is the information a system tracks within one session, such as the current task and recent steps. Memory is what it keeps across sessions, such as user preferences or past decisions. Models do not remember anything by default, so both have to be stored outside the model and added back into the context when needed.
resources: A Practical Guide to Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents - Towards Data Science
Memory Management in AI Agents - LangChain
State, Memory, and Context in Agents: How AI Keeps Track of What You Asked - Medium
The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent Needs

topics.title: Meta
topics.description: Meta develops the Llama family of open-source large language models. The latest release, Llama 4, comes in Maverick and Scout variants with strong multimodal and long-context capabilities. Llama models are freely available for research and commercial use, providing transparency in training data and architecture without vendor lock-in.

topics.title: Model Size & Cost
topics.description: Models come in different sizes, from small and fast ones to large frontier models. Larger models are usually more capable but cost more per token and respond more slowly. Many applications use a small model for simple tasks and a large one only for hard requests. Pricing is normally charged per input and output token, so prompt length affects the bill.
resources: Beyond vibes: How to properly select the right LLM for the right task - AWS
The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost - DigitalOcean

topics.title: Model Weights / Parameters
topics.description: Weights, also called parameters, are the numbers a model learns during training. They determine how it responds to any input. Bigger models have more parameters, often billions. Prompting does not change them, while fine-tuning does.
resources: Understanding Tokens and Parameters in Model Training - Functionize

topics.title: Multi-Agent Context Sharing
topics.description: In multi-agent systems, context sharing decides what information passes between agents. Sharing too little leaves an agent without what it needs, while sharing too much brings back the clutter that isolation was meant to remove. Common approaches are passing short summaries or structured results, using shared memory or files, and giving each agent only the parts relevant to its job.
resources: How to Implement Multi-Agent Context Sharing Patterns - Fast.io
Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context - arXiv
Multi Agent Systems Explained: How AI Agents & LLMs Work Together

topics.title: Multimodal Inputs
topics.description: Multimodal inputs let a model work with images, PDFs, audio and sometimes video, as well as text. Prompts should say what to look at and what to extract, for example "list the line items and totals from this invoice." Check results on small or low-quality details, since models can misread them.
resources: What Is Multimodal AI? A Complete Introduction - Splunk

topics.title: One-Shot / Few-Shot
topics.description: One-shot and few-shot prompting include one or several worked examples in the prompt before the real input. The model copies the pattern, which helps with output format, tone and unusual tasks. Examples should be consistent and cover varied cases, because the model tends to imitate them closely.
resources: What is few shot prompting? - IBM
Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering: Smarter AI with RAG & Agents

topics.title: Open vs Closed Models
topics.description: Closed models, such as GPT, Claude and Gemini, are used through a provider's API and their weights are not public. Open-weights models, such as Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek and Mistral, can be downloaded, self-hosted and fine-tuned. Closed models usually lead on capability and are simple to start with. Open models give more control over cost, privacy and customization.
resources: Open Source vs Closed LLMs Guide - HatchWorks
Open-source Models vs. Closed-Source Models: A Simple Guide - Koat
Open Source vs Closed AI: LLMs, Agents & the AI Stack Explained

topics.title: OpenAI
topics.description: OpenAI develops leading language models including GPT-5.4, o3, and Codex, setting industry standards for prompt engineering. Their API provides access to frontier models with configurable parameters, and their Agents SDK enables building autonomous AI systems. The OpenAI Cookbook and platform documentation are key references for prompt engineering best practices.

topics.title: Output Format
topics.description: Output format is the shape you want the response to take: plain prose, a list, a table, Markdown, JSON or XML. Stating the format clearly, and showing an example, makes the response easier to read or parse. Tone and style can be controlled in the same way, by describing them in the instructions.
resources: Mastering Prompt Engineering: Format, Length, and Audience - Techlasi

topics.title: Output Limits
topics.description: Output limits control how much a model writes and where it stops. They keep responses short enough for your use case and keep cost and latency down. The main tools are a maximum token count, stop sequences and, for reasoning models, an effort setting.
resources: General Tips for Designing Prompts - DAIR.AI

topics.title: Output Validation
topics.description: Output validation checks a model's response before it is shown to a user or passed to another system. Checks include validating JSON against a schema, filtering unsafe or off-topic content, and testing values against business rules. If a check fails, the system can retry, repair the output or send it to a person.
resources: How to use the moderation API - OpenAI Cookbook
How to Build Safe AI Agents: Best Practices for Guardrails - Medium

topics.title: Presence Penalty
topics.description: Presence penalty reduces the likelihood of repeating tokens that have already appeared in the text, encouraging diverse vocabulary usage. Unlike frequency penalty which considers how often tokens appear, presence penalty applies the same penalty to any previously used token, promoting varied content and creativity.
resources: Presence Penalty - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum

topics.title: Prompt Caching
topics.description: Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix between requests. It lowers cost and latency when the beginning of the prompt stays the same, such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents. To benefit, put stable content first and changing content, such as the user's message, last.
resources: What is Prompt Caching? Optimize LLM Latency with AI Transformers

topics.title: Prompt Chaining
topics.description: Prompt chaining splits a large task into a sequence of smaller prompts, where the output of one step becomes the input of the next. Each step is simpler, easier to test and easier to fix. A typical chain is extract, then analyze, then write. You can also add a check between steps to stop errors from carrying forward.
resources: Chain complex prompts for stronger performance - Anthropic

topics.title: Prompt Debiasing
topics.description: Prompt debiasing involves techniques to reduce unwanted biases in LLM outputs by carefully crafting prompts. This includes using neutral language, diverse examples, and explicit instructions to avoid stereotypes or unfair representations. Effective debiasing helps ensure AI outputs are fairer, inclusive, and more representative across different groups and perspectives.

topics.title: Prompt Ensembling
topics.description: Prompt ensembling asks the same question in several different ways, or with several models, and combines the answers by voting or merging. Different phrasings make different mistakes, so the combined result is often more reliable than any single one. It trades extra cost and latency for accuracy.

topics.title: Prompt Evaluation
topics.description: Prompt evaluation is measuring how well a prompt performs on a set of test cases. Instead of judging a few outputs by eye, you run the prompt on many inputs and score the results. It shows whether a change really helps and where the prompt fails.
resources: Define success criteria and build evaluations - Anthropic
LLM evaluation: a beginner's guide - Evidently AI
A pragmatic guide to LLM evals for devs - The Pragmatic Engineer
Welcome to the LLM evaluation course

topics.title: Prompt Injection
topics.description: Prompt injection is an attack where text in the input makes the model ignore its original instructions. It can be typed directly by a user, or hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page, an email or a document. It is hard to fully prevent, so defenses include separating trusted from untrusted content, limiting what the model can do and checking outputs.
resources: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections - Anthropic
Prompt Injection: Hands-on Exercise Against a Live Assistant
What Is a Prompt Injection Attack?

topics.title: Prompt Management
topics.description: Prompt management is how a team stores, versions, reviews and monitors the prompts used in a product. Prompts are treated like code: they have owners, history and tests. This makes changes safe and easy to roll back, and shows how a prompt performs in production.
resources: A guide to LLM debugging, tracing, and monitoring - Weights & Biases

topics.title: Prompt Structure
topics.description: Prompt structure is how you organize the parts of a prompt so the model can tell them apart. A common layout puts the role or task first, then the context or data, then the output requirements. Separating sections clearly reduces confusion, especially when the prompt contains user-supplied text.
resources: Prompt Structure and Key Parts - LearnPrompting
Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance? - arXiv

topics.title: Prompt Templates
topics.description: A prompt template is a prompt with placeholders, such as `{{customer_name}}`, that your code fills in at run time. It keeps the fixed instructions separate from the changing input, so the same prompt can be reused and tested. Templates also make versioning and evaluation easier, since only the variables change between runs.

topics.title: Prompt Tuning
topics.description: Prompt tuning is a method for adapting large AI models to new tasks without changing the model itself. Instead of retraining billions of parameters, it learns a small set of special vectors called “soft prompts” that are added to the input. These act like hidden instructions that guide the model toward the desired behavior while keeping the original model unchanged. This approach is much more efficient in terms of computation and storage, making it a practical choice for customizing models across many different tasks.
resources: Prompt tune a Granite model in Python using watsonx

topics.title: Prompt Tuning
topics.description: Prompt tuning trains a small set of learned vectors, called a soft prompt, that is added to the model's input while the model's weights stay frozen. It differs from writing prompts by hand, because the learned values are not readable text. It needs access to training and model internals, so it is mostly used with open models.
resources: Prompt tune a Granite model in Python using watsonx - IBM
Prompt Engineering vs Prompt Tuning: A Detailed Explanation - Medium

topics.title: Prompt Versioning
topics.description: Prompt versioning means keeping a history of each prompt change, with the date, the reason and its evaluation results. When quality drops, you can compare versions and roll back. Recording what you tried and why also saves others from repeating failed experiments.
resources: A guide to LLM debugging, tracing, and monitoring - Weights & Biases

topics.title: Prompt vs Context Eng.
topics.description: Prompt engineering focuses on the wording and structure of the instructions you send to a model. Context engineering decides what information goes into the model's context window at each step, including documents, tool results, memory and history. The prompt is one part of the context. For a single chat request the prompt matters most, while for agents and RAG applications the quality of the surrounding context usually decides the result.
resources: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic
Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering - DataHub
Context engineering vs. prompt engineering - Elastic
Beyond Prompting: The Power of Context Engineering - Towards Data Science
Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering: Smarter AI with RAG & Agents

topics.title: Prompting Approaches
topics.description: Prompting approaches are the basic ways of shaping a request to a model. They differ in how many examples you give and where the instructions and background sit. The most common are zero-shot, few-shot, system, role and contextual prompting. Most real prompts combine several of them.

topics.title: RAG & Dynamic Filters
topics.description: RAG retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt. Dynamic filters narrow the search with metadata such as date, source, user or document type, so the results are relevant to the request. Good retrieval depends on chunking, embeddings and often a reranking step. Retrieving less but more relevant material usually beats loading everything.
resources: 4 context engineering strategies every AI engineer needs to know - Owain Lewis
Is RAG Dead? The Rise of Context Engineering and Semantic Layers for Agentic AI - Towards Data Science
Chunking Strategies for LLM Applications - Pinecone

topics.title: RAG
topics.description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches relevant documents from an external source at query time and adds them to the prompt. The model then answers using that material instead of relying only on its training data. It is commonly used to give a model current or private knowledge and to reduce made-up answers.
resources: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation? - Google Cloud

topics.title: ReAct Prompting
topics.description: ReAct (Reason and Act) prompting enables LLMs to solve complex tasks by combining reasoning with external tool interactions. It follows a thought-action-observation loop: analyze the problem, perform actions using external APIs, review results, and iterate until solved. Useful for research, multi-step problems, and tasks requiring current data.

topics.title: ReAct Prompting
topics.description: ReAct prompting makes the model alternate between reasoning and acting. It writes a thought about what to do, takes an action such as a search or tool call, reads the result and repeats until it can answer. This loop is the basis of most agents. Modern tool calling has largely replaced hand-written ReAct prompts, but the pattern is the same.
resources: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
ReAct Systems: Enhancing LLMs with Reasoning and Action - LearnPrompting

topics.title: Reasoning Models
topics.description: Reasoning models spend extra tokens thinking through a problem before they give a final answer. This makes them stronger at math, logic, coding and multi-step planning, but slower and more expensive than standard models. They need different prompting: clear goals work better than step-by-step instructions, since they already plan their own steps.
resources: What is a reasoning model? - IBM
How do thinking and reasoning models work?

topics.title: Reasoning Techniques
topics.description: Reasoning techniques are prompting methods that help a model work through problems step by step or check its own answers. Some change how the model reasons, such as chain of thought, while others improve reliability by comparing or reviewing several outputs. Reasoning models do much of this internally, so these techniques matter most for standard models.

topics.title: Regression Testing
topics.description: Regression testing reruns your eval set every time a prompt, model or context setup changes. It catches cases where a change that fixes one problem breaks something that used to work. Running it automatically on each change keeps quality from drifting without anyone noticing.
resources: Watch the language: A tutorial on regression testing for LLMs - Evidently AI
Regression Testing for LLMs: Golden Datasets Explained

topics.title: Repetition Controls
topics.description: Repetition controls discourage a model from repeating itself. Frequency penalty lowers the chance of a token the more often it has appeared, while presence penalty lowers the chance of any token that has already appeared. They push the model toward new words and topics. Availability depends on the provider, and they are rarely needed on current models.
resources: Frequency Penalty - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum
Stop the LLM From Rambling: Using Penalties to Control Repetition - DEV
What are LLM Presence and Frequency Penalties?

topics.title: Repetition Penalties
topics.description: Repetition penalties discourage LLMs from repeating words or phrases by reducing the probability of selecting previously used tokens. This includes frequency penalty (scales with usage count) and presence penalty (applies equally to any used token). These parameters improve output quality by promoting vocabulary diversity and preventing redundant phrasing.
resources: Tips for Writing Better Prompts - LearnPrompting

topics.title: Role Prompting
topics.description: Role prompting assigns the model a persona or job, such as "You are a senior data analyst." It shapes tone, vocabulary and the perspective of the answer. On current models the gain in accuracy is small, so it is most useful for style and point of view. It is often placed in the system prompt but also works in a user message.
resources: Beyond Basics: Contextual & Role Prompting That Actually Works - Medium
Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering: Smarter AI with RAG & Agents

topics.title: Sampling Parameters
topics.description: Sampling parameters control how a model picks the next token from its probability distribution. They set how random or repetitive the output is. The main ones are temperature, top-K, top-P and repetition controls. Some newer models fix or limit these settings, so check what your model allows.
resources: LLM Parameters Explained: A Practical Guide with Examples - LearnPrompting

topics.title: Self-Consistency
topics.description: Self-consistency runs the same reasoning prompt several times with some randomness, then picks the answer that appears most often. It improves accuracy on tasks with one correct answer, such as math problems. The cost is more calls, so it raises both price and latency.

topics.title: Self-Evaluation
topics.description: Self-evaluation asks a model to review its own output against criteria and then fix problems. A typical pattern is draft, critique, revise. It can catch obvious errors and improve quality, but models are often overconfident about their own mistakes. Tests, sources and other external checks are more reliable when they are available.

topics.title: Spec-First Prompts
topics.description: A spec-first prompt means writing a short specification before asking a coding agent to build something. It states the goal, constraints, relevant files and how you will check that the work is done. Many people also ask the agent for a plan and review it before any code is written. This reduces rework and keeps the agent from guessing.
resources: Explore first, then plan, then code - Claude Code
How to use Plan Mode - Claude Code
What Actually Is Claude Code's Plan Mode?

topics.title: Step-Back Prompting
topics.description: Step-back prompting improves LLM performance by first asking a general question related to the specific task, then using that answer to inform the final response. This technique activates relevant background knowledge before attempting the specific problem. For example, before writing a video game level storyline, first ask "What are key settings for engaging first-person shooter levels?" then use those insights to create the specific storyline. This approach reduces biases and improves accuracy by grounding responses in broader principles.

topics.title: Stop Sequences
topics.description: Stop sequences are strings that make the model stop generating as soon as it produces them, such as a closing tag or a line of dashes. They give clean boundaries to the output and prevent extra text. They are useful for structured formats and for few-shot patterns where the model might otherwise keep going.
resources: Stop Sequence - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum

topics.title: Structured Outputs
topics.description: Structured outputs are responses in a fixed format such as JSON, XML or a table, so code can read them reliably. You can request them in the prompt by describing the fields and showing an example. This works most of the time but is not guaranteed, so the output should still be validated before use.
resources: Structured Outputs - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum
Generating Structured Outputs from LLMs - Towards Data Science

topics.title: System Prompting
topics.description: A system prompt is a set of instructions given before the conversation that sets the model's behavior, rules and output format. It usually holds the role, constraints, tone and background for the task. Instructions in it normally take priority over user messages, although this is not a guarantee against conflicting or malicious input.
resources: User prompts vs. system prompts: What's the difference? - Regie.ai

topics.title: Temperature
topics.description: Temperature controls how random the output is. Low values make the model pick the most likely tokens, giving more consistent and predictable answers. High values allow more variety, which helps with brainstorming and creative writing. Even at low temperature the same prompt can give slightly different replies.
resources: What Temperature Means in Natural Language Processing and AI - The New Stack

topics.title: Tokens
topics.description: Tokens are the pieces of text a model reads and writes, usually word fragments a few characters long. A word can be one token or several, and in English a token averages roughly three quarters of a word. Pricing, speed and context limits are all measured in tokens.
resources: What Are Tokens in LLMs and Why They Matter - LLM Guides
Explaining Tokens: the Language and Currency of AI - NVIDIA

topics.title: Tool Calling
topics.description: Tool calling, also called function calling, lets a model request that your code run a function with specific arguments. You describe each tool with a name, a purpose and a JSON Schema for its inputs. The model replies with a tool request, your code executes it and returns the result, and the model uses it in its answer. Clear tool names and descriptions strongly affect how well the model picks the right one.
resources: A Comprehensive Guide to Function Calling in LLMs - The New Stack
LLM Function Calling - AI Tools Deep Dive

topics.title: Tools & Agents
topics.description: Tools let a model act beyond generating text, for example by searching, querying a database or running code. Agents use tools in a loop and decide their own steps. Prompting for them means describing tools clearly, setting limits and keeping the context focused. Simpler fixed workflows are often more reliable than a full agent.

topics.title: Top-K & Top-P
topics.description: Top-K limits the choice of next token to the K most likely ones. Top-P, also called nucleus sampling, limits it to the smallest group of tokens whose combined probability reaches P. Both cut off unlikely tokens and reduce odd output. They are usually adjusted instead of temperature, not together with it.
resources: Top K - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum
How do Top-k and Top-p Sampling work? - Outcome School
What are the LLM's Top-P + Top-K?

topics.title: Top-P
topics.description: Top-P (nucleus sampling) selects tokens from the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds threshold P. Unlike Top-K's fixed number, Top-P dynamically adjusts based on probability distribution. Low values (0.1-0.5) produce focused outputs, medium (0.6-0.9) balance creativity and coherence, high (0.9-0.99) enable creative diversity.
resources: Top P - LLM Parameter Guide - Vellum

topics.title: Tree of Thoughts (ToT)
topics.description: Tree of thoughts lets a model explore several reasoning paths, evaluate them and go back when one fails, instead of following a single chain. It suits planning and puzzle problems where the first idea is often wrong. It needs many model calls per task, so it is mostly used in research and special cases.

topics.title: What is a Prompt?
topics.description: A prompt is the input you give a model to get a response. It usually combines an instruction, optional background or data, examples and a description of the output format you want. Clearer and more specific prompts produce more predictable results.

topics.title: xAI
topics.description: xAI develops Grok, a conversational AI model with real-time web access and integration with X (Twitter). The latest model, Grok 4.20, features a 2M token context window, agentic tool calling, and industry-leading low hallucination rates. Grok focuses on delivering truthful, unfiltered responses with strict prompt adherence.

topics.title: Zero-Shot
topics.description: Zero-shot prompting means asking the model to do a task with no examples, relying only on the instruction. It works well for common tasks such as summarizing, translating or answering simple questions. It is the usual starting point, and you add examples when the output is not what you want.
resources: Zero-shot, One-shot and Few-shot Prompting Explained
